# Overview & Orientation {background-color="#0f172a"}

## Executive Summary {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
### The 30-Year Cardiomyocyte Paradox
- **The Central Paradigm**: Post-myocardial infarction heart failure (HF) alters sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ handling and excitation-contraction coupling.
- **The Controversy**: Over 18 published studies report **contradictory findings** for virtually every Ca2+ kinetic parameter (some report increases, others report decreases, others find no change).
- **The Real Cause**: It is **not** biological model differences. It is **statistical disaggregation**—treating cells or sparks from the same heart as independent data points ($N \times m$).

::: {.callout-note}
### Core Finding (Sikkel et al., 2017)
"Ca2+ fluxes in isolated cardiomyocytes show severe clustering (ICC up to 58%). Standard statistical tests underestimate standard errors, resulting in a **150% overstatement** of statistically significant changes."
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">150%</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Overstatement of Significance</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">Standard naive t-tests identified 5 of 10 comparisons as significant; hierarchical models showed only 2 were real.</div>
</div>

<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">58%</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Peak Intraclass Correlation</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">Observed in Ca2+ spark amplitude (LogAmp), demonstrating extreme clustering at cell and animal levels.</div>
</div>

<div class="stat-card">
  <div class="stat-number">200 &rarr; 19</div>
  <div class="stat-label">Effective Sample Size ($N_{\text{eff}}$)</div>
  <div class="stat-desc">With 10 rats and 20 cells each ($\text{ICC} = 0.5$), the effective biological sample size collapses from 200 to only 19.</div>
</div>
:::
:::

# The Heart Failure Controversy {#hf-controversy background-color="#0f172a"}

## Conflicting Literature in Post-MI Heart Failure {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Left Anterior Descending (LAD) Model
- The standard rat coronary artery ligation model has been used for over 50 years to study ischemic cardiomyopathy (Johns & Olson, 1954).
- **Whole-Organ Level**: Remarkable consistency across laboratories (ejection fraction drops from ~83% to ~40%, heart weight:body weight ratio increases by ~25%).
- **Cellular & Subcellular Level**: **Complete discordance**.
  - Does Ca2+ transient amplitude increase or decrease?
  - Does transient decay slow down or accelerate?
  - Does SR Ca2+ content deplete or overload?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Flawed "Biological" Explanations

Before Sikkel et al., researchers proposed ad-hoc biological rationales:

::: {.incremental}
1. *"Compensated vs. De-compensated Phases"*: Refuted by timeline meta-analysis (no temporal trend from 3 to 18 weeks post-MI).
2. *"Myofilament Desensitization Overriding Ca2+"*: Invoked when contractile dysfunction was found alongside enhanced transients.
3. *"Model & Species Artifacts"*: Refuted because conflicting directions exist within the exact same rat LAD ligation protocol!
:::

::: {.callout-important}
### The Unexamined Culprit
The statistical methods treated technical cell replicates as independent observations, generating false significance out of random noise.
:::
:::
:::

## Literature Meta-Analysis: Table 1 Summary {.compact-slide}

Summary of reported changes in electrically evoked Ca2+ transients across 18 landmark rat post-MI studies:

| Parameter | Increased ($\uparrow$) | Unchanged ($\leftrightarrow$) | Decreased ($\downarrow$) | Total Studies | Consensus Status |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Transient Amplitude** | 5 | 5 | 3 | 13 | ❌ **Direct Conflict** |
| **Transient Decay Time** | 11 | 6 | 0 | 17 | ⚠️ Broad Conflict |
| **SR Ca2+ Content** | 1 | 3 | 1 | 5 | ❌ **Opposite Directions** |
| **Diastolic [Ca2+]i** | 4 | 4 | 0 | 8 | ⚠️ 50/50 Split |

::: {.callout-caution}
### The Cost of Statistical Disaggregation
When standard statistical tests are applied to clustered data, spurious statistical significance is generated in arbitrary directions depending on which specific animal's cells dominated that day's preparation.
:::

# Hierarchical Structure of Myocyte Studies {#myocyte-hierarchy background-color="#0f172a"}

## Anatomy of the Experimental Hierarchy (Figure 1) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Figure 1: Hierarchical structure of data from isolated cardiomyocyte studies](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/de7c/5852514/ade49ab4620f/cvx151f1.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Multi-Level Nesting Architecture
- **Multiple Cells per Isolation**: Multiple cardiomyocytes originate from each heart isolation.
- **Within-Heart Correlation**: Differences between animals and slight daily variations in isolation quality mean measurements in **Cell A** are more similar to **Cell B** (same heart) than to **Cell C** (different heart).
- **Subcellular Sparks**: Individual sparks recorded within a cell exhibit an additional third level of hierarchy.

::: {.callout-note}
### The Independence Violation
A fundamental condition of common statistical tests (e.g. $t$-tests and ANOVA)—**independence of observations**—is therefore contravened.
:::
:::
:::

## Why Do Cardiomyocytes Cluster Within Hearts? {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Biological & Isolation Batch Effects
In cardiac cellular physiology, cells isolated on the same day from the same heart share:
- **Enzymatic Digestion Kinetics**: Batch variations in collagenase, protease activity, perfusion pressure, and digestion time.
- **Dye Loading & Temperature**: Exact micro-variations in Fura-2AM / Fluo-4AM de-esterification and bath temperature ($37^\circ\text{C}$).
- **Hemodynamic Milieu**: Animal-specific neurohormonal tone, infarct size, and systemic adrenergic drive.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Subcellular Stochasticity in Sparks
- Ca2+ sparks arise from stochastic openings of ryanodine receptor (RyR) clusters.
- Because spark morphology varies within a cell, investigators assumed individual sparks could be treated as independent data points!
- Sikkel et al. demonstrate that **sparks show profound clustering at the cell level** ($\text{ICC} = 58\%$).
- Local t-tubule architecture and sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ load create cell-specific spark microenvironments.
:::
:::

# Clustering, ICC & Effective Sample Size {#icc-framework background-color="#0f172a"}

## Quantifying Clustering: The Intraclass Correlation (Figure 2) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 2: Intraclass correlation in cardiomyocyte studies](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/de7c/5852514/6ce0a5998b71/cvx151f2.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Clustering Magnitude & Correction
The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient ($\text{ICC}$) quantifies the proportion of total variance attributable to the heart/isolation:

$$\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{rat}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{rat}} + \sigma^2_{\text{cell}}}$$

- **Top Panel (High ICC $\approx 90\%$)**: Cells cluster tightly in each heart. Large correction required.
- **Middle Panel (Intermediate ICC $\approx 50\%$)**: Moderate clustering.
- **Bottom Panel (Low ICC $\approx 10\%$)**: High proportion of total variability coming from each individual heart.

::: {.callout-important}
### Standard Error Deflation
$$\text{SE}_{\text{hierarchical}} = \text{SE}_{\text{naive}} \times \sqrt{1 + (m - 1)\times \text{ICC}}$$
:::
:::
:::

## Sikkel's Effective Sample Size Equation {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### The Formulation
For an experiment with $n$ animals and $m$ cells per animal:

$$N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n \times m}{1 + (m - 1) \times \text{ICC}}$$

- **Limiting Case 1 ($\text{ICC} \to 0$)**: $N_{\text{eff}} \to n \times m$ (all cells independent).
- **Limiting Case 2 ($\text{ICC} \to 1$)**: $N_{\text{eff}} \to n$ (cells redundant).

### The Worked Example (Sikkel et al.)
- Consider $n = 10$ animals, $m = 20$ cells each ($n \times m = 200$).
- If $\text{ICC} = 50\%$ ($0.50$):
  $$N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{200}{1 + (19 \times 0.5)} = \frac{200}{1 + 9.5} = \frac{200}{10.5} \approx \mathbf{19.0}$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Power Calculations Must Use $N_{\text{eff}}$
```{r}
#| label: neff-table
m_cells <- c(5, 10, 20, 50)
iccs <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75)
n_rats <- 10

neff_df <- outer(m_cells, iccs, function(m, r) {
  round((n_rats * m) / (1 + (m - 1) * r), 1)
})
colnames(neff_df) <- paste0("ICC = ", iccs * 100, "%")
rownames(neff_df) <- paste0("m = ", m_cells, " cells (Total ", n_rats * m_cells, ")")
knitr::kable(neff_df, caption = "Effective Sample Size (N_eff) for 10 Rats")
```

::: {.callout-caution}
### Critical Rule for Study Design
Standard power calculators assume independent observations. If your target sample size is 19 animals, collecting 200 cells from 10 animals only achieves $N_{\text{eff}} = 19$.
:::
:::
:::

# Two-Level Hierarchy: Ca2+ Transients {#transients-analysis background-color="#0f172a"}

## Ca2+ Transient Morphology: Table 2 Results {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Empirical Analysis (76 Control vs. 79 HF Cells)
```{r}
#| label: table2-display
t2 <- cvx_data$table2_transients
t2_disp <- t2[, c("variable", "icc_pct", "common_p", "hier_p", "p_superior_fit")]
colnames(t2_disp) <- c("Morphological Variable", "ICC (%)", "Common p", "Hierarchical p", "Superior Fit")
knitr::kable(t2_disp, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

::: {.callout-important}
### P-value Reversal in Time to 50% Peak
- Common t-test: $p = 0.018$ (statistically significant prolongation!).
- Hierarchical test: $p = 0.109$ (non-significant!).
- The apparent kinetic prolongation was completely spurious.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Mechanistic Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
1. **Significant Clustering Everywhere**: ICC ranged from $12\%$ to $47\%$. For every variable, hierarchical modeling fit significantly better ($p < 0.05$).
2. **Standard Errors Were Artificially Deflated**: For tau of decay, hierarchical $\text{SE} = 17.7$ vs. common $\text{SE} = 8.55$ (a 2-fold deflation!).
3. **The Only Real Difference**: Transient amplitude is significantly higher in HF ($p = 0.010$), driven entirely by peak systolic ratio ($p = 0.046$).
:::
:::
:::

## The "Goldilocks" Confidence Interval (Figure 3) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 3: Correction for clustering produced by hierarchical tests](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/de7c/5852514/e97781b6cbc8/cvx151f3.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### The "Goldilocks" Confidence Interval
- **Disaggregated CI** ($n \times m$ independent data points):
  $$\text{CI} = \pm 1.96 \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n \times m}} \quad \text{(Erroneously Narrow)}$$
- **Aggregated CI** ($m$ rat averages as data points):
  $$\text{CI} = \pm 1.96 \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}} \quad \text{(Erroneously Wide)}$$
- **Hierarchical Technique**:
  Calculates the SEM based on the exact degree of clustering ($\text{ICC}$), giving the true, unbiased **"Goldilocks" confidence interval**.
:::
:::

## Ca2+ Transient Clustering & CI Correction (Figure 4) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 4: Clustering of time to 50% peak transient amplitude](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/de7c/5852514/aa5872a539f0/cvx151f4.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Clustered Transients in Heart Failure
- **Panel A (Clustering by Rat)**: Time to 50% peak for each cell (grey dots) across 10 control and 10 HF rats. Data are visibly clustered within hearts ($\text{ICC} = 12\%$).
- **Panel B (95% CI Comparison)**: 
  - **Common Test (Red)**: Artificially narrow CI excludes zero ($p = 0.018$).
  - **Hierarchical Test (Green)**: Corrected CI spans zero ($p = 0.109$).

::: {.callout-tip}
### Resolution of Literature Conflict
Failing to account for rat-level clustering created the false appearance that Ca2+ transients are delayed in HF.
:::
:::
:::

# Three-Level Hierarchy: Ca2+ Sparks {#sparks-analysis background-color="#0f172a"}

## Three-Level Spark Architecture: Table 3 Results {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### 696 Sparks Across 39 Cells from 12 Rats
```{r}
#| label: table3-display
t3 <- cvx_data$table3_sparks
t3_disp <- t3[, c("variable", "icc_pct", "hierarchy_level", "common_p", "hier_p")]
colnames(t3_disp) <- c("Spark Variable", "ICC (%)", "Best Model", "Common p", "Hierarchical p")
knitr::kable(t3_disp, align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

::: {.callout-danger}
### Catastrophic Overstatement Exposed
The common test claimed **LogAmp was highly significant ($p < 0.001$)** and **LogFDHM was significant ($p = 0.023$)**. 
Under the 3-level hierarchical model, **neither is significant ($p = 0.239$ and $p = 0.778$)**!
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Why Spark Hierarchies Matter
- Sparks are nested inside **cells**, which are nested inside **rats**.
- **LogAmp**: Exhibits an astonishing **$\text{ICC} = 58\%$** clustering. 
  - Standard error under naive test: $0.0090$.
  - Standard error under 3-level model: $0.0641$ (**a 7-fold increase!**).
- **Result**: Not a single spark morphology parameter is significantly altered in HF!
:::
:::

## Multi-Level Clustering of Ca2+ Sparks (Figure 5) {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Figure 5: Multi-level clustering of spark logAmp](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/de7c/5852514/8bbda5b765c4/cvx151f5.jpg){width=100%}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Multi-Tiered Spark Architecture
- **Panel A (Cell-Level Clustering)**: Sparks from 5 cells of a single rat heart show marked cellular clustering.
- **Panel B (Rat-Level Clustering)**: Sparks further cluster across individual rats.
- **Panel C (95% CI Comparison)**:
  - **Common Test (Red)**: With 2 levels of uncorrected clustering ($\text{ICC} = 58\%$), difference appears highly significant ($p < 0.001$).
  - **3-Level Hierarchical (Green)**: Standard error widens 7-fold; CI properly spans zero ($p = 0.239$).

::: {.callout-important}
### True Spark Reality
None of the spark variables (amplitude, width, duration, frequency) differ between HF and control. Standard methods manufactured illusory significance.
:::
:::
:::

# Aggregation vs. Disaggregation {#analytical-approaches background-color="#0f172a"}

## The Flaws of Crude Alternatives {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1. Disaggregation (Splitting)
- Treat all $n \times m$ points as independent.
- **The Fatal Flaw**: Falsely small SE, falsely small confidence intervals, falsely small p-values.
- **Isolation Bias**: Overweights "good isolation days" where many cells were easily harvested from 1 or 2 animals.

::: {.callout-danger}
### The 150% Error Rate
In Sikkel et al.'s dataset, disaggregation claimed 5 of 10 comparisons were significant, when only 2 were real.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 2. Aggregation (Lumping)
- Average all data points from an animal into a single mean.
- **The Fatal Flaw**: Excessively conservative; collapses 696 sparks into just 12 numbers.
- **Isolation Bias**: Overweights "bad isolation days" by giving equal weight to 1 or 2 sickly cells as to 50 healthy cells!

::: {.callout-tip}
### The Hierarchical Mixed Model Solution
Weights each animal's contribution by its precision, preserves all individual data points, and guarantees honest type I error control.
:::
:::
:::

## Method Comparison Matrix {.compact-slide}

| Feature | Disaggregation (Common Practice) | Aggregation (Animal Means) | Hierarchical Linear Mixed Models |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Data Unit** | Pooled cells or sparks | Animal averages | All observations + cluster IDs |
| **False-Positive Risk** | **Severe (150% overstatement) ❌** | Controlled (Nominal 5%) ✅ | **Controlled (Nominal 5%) ✅** |
| **Statistical Power** | Spurious / Invalid | Low (excessively conservative) | **Optimal (Maximum valid power) ✅** |
| **"Good vs Bad Days"** | Biased toward good days | Biased toward bad days | **Unbiased (Precision-weighted) ✅** |
| **Handles 3-Level Data?** | No | Destroys data structure | **Yes (Rat + Cell + Spark) ✅** |
| **Software Accessibility** | Ubiquitous (Excel, basic t-tests) | Easy (Average in Excel $\to$ t-test) | **Freely available in R (`lmerTest`, `nlme`)** |

::: {.callout-note}
### Key Takeaway
Hierarchical modeling is not merely a "p-value penalty." It is a structural framework that matches the physical reality of the biological laboratory.
:::

# The Open-Source R Toolkit {#r-toolkit background-color="#0f172a"}

## Sikkel et al.'s Free Open-Source Solution {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Two-Level Hierarchy (`ratonly.Rmd`)
For Ca2+ transients or slice contractility with rat-level clustering:

```r
library(lmerTest)

# Fit linear mixed-effects model
fit_transient <- lmer(
  time_to_peak ~ condition + (1 | rat_id), 
  data = transient_data
)

# Extract Satterthwaite-corrected ANOVA table
anova(fit_transient)

# Pairwise differences with honest standard errors
difflsmeans(fit_transient)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Three-Level Hierarchy (`ratandcell.Rmd`)
For Ca2+ sparks with both cell- and rat-level clustering:

```r
library(lmerTest)

# Fit three-level nested model
fit_spark <- lmer(
  log_amp ~ condition + (1 | rat_id) + (1 | cell_id), 
  data = spark_data
)

# Test whether 3-level model improves fit over 2-level
fit_spark_2level <- lmer(
  log_amp ~ condition + (1 | rat_id), 
  data = spark_data
)
anova(fit_spark_2level, fit_spark) # Likelihood Ratio Test
```
:::
:::

## Visualizing Clustering in R {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### R Code for SuperPlots
```r
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(spark_df, aes(x = condition, y = log_amp, color = rat_id)) +
  # 1. Jitter individual sparks as semi-transparent dots
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2), 
             alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  # 2. Overlay animal summary diamonds
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, 
               size = 4, fill = "black", color = "white") +
  # 3. Superimpose condition mean and animal-level SE
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", 
               width = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Four Output Tables from R Scripts
The scripts provided by Sikkel et al. generate four automated tables:
1. **Model Comparison Table**: Common vs. Hierarchical $p$-values, $\text{ICC}$, and $\chi^2_{-2\text{LL}}$ test for superior fit.
2. **Point Estimates Table**: Estimated marginal means with corrected $95\%$ confidence intervals.
3. **Pairwise Differences Table**: Pairwise contrast tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
4. **Variance Components Table**: Variance partitioned between rat, cell, and residual.
:::
:::

# Synthesis & Laboratory Guidelines {#synthesis-guidelines background-color="#0f172a"}

## 5 Practical Rules for Isolated Cell Studies {.compact-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
### 1. Test for Clustering First
Never assume cellular data are independent. Always calculate the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient ($\text{ICC}$) and perform a $\chi^2_{-2\text{LL}}$ likelihood ratio test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
### 2. Base Power Calculations on $N_{\text{eff}}$
Do not use raw cell counts ($n \times m$) in power calculations. Multiply your target animal count by $(1 + (m - 1)\text{ICC})$ to find the true required sample size.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
### 3. Transparent Multi-Level Reporting
State in all figure legends: *"Data represent $k = 696$ sparks across $m = 39$ cells from $n = 12$ rats. Analyzed via 3-level hierarchical mixed models."*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-caution}
### 4. Resist Binary P-Value Fetishism
Focus on effect sizes and honest $95\%$ confidence intervals. Recognize that standard $t$-tests produce artificially narrow intervals that create illusory significance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
### 5. Adopt Cost-Free Tools
Use R (`lmerTest`, `nlme`) or GraphPad Prism's Nested ANOVA tools. Do not let lack of specialized software justify disaggregation.
:::
:::
:::
